title: Immigration
question: Which record's position, as its evidence shows it, is closer to admitting more immigrants and refugees and widening the rights of migrants already in the country?
weighing: Judge the changes a record supports or opposes, whether it enacted them in government, voted on them, pressed for them, or seeks them, by their direction and size. Judge the size of what a record supports, not what it had the power to achieve: a record that backs every change in one direction put before it and seeks larger ones supports more change in that direction than one that enacted smaller changes. The tier shows how firmly an item commits the actor, not how large the change is; where a record's items point in opposite directions, the higher tier governs. A vote against a change counts as support for what the change would have removed, unless the record shows it opposed the change for not going far enough, for example by backing stricter or wider versions of it; then it counts as support for going further. The immigration rules a record inherited are not part of its position.
highPole: more immigrants and refugees admitted, with wider rights once in the country
lowPole: fewer admitted, with stricter enforcement, detention and removal

slots.heading: Changes to who may come and stay in the period
Changes to enforcement, detention, and removal in the period
Changes to migrants' rights and the path to citizenship in the period

items.text: Voted for a law doubling the yearly number of refugees resettled from abroad and opening a work visa for any job offer paying at least the minimum wage, raising new arrivals by about 1 percent of the population a year.
Voted for a law ending immigration detention of families with children and limiting any other immigration detention to 30 days.
Voted for a law giving residents without legal status who have lived in the country for five years a path to permanent residence, about 2 percent of the population.
Voted against a law ending citizenship by birth for children of parents without legal status.
Pledged to let asylum seekers work from the day they apply.
Voted for a law raising skilled work visas by about 20 percent while cutting visas for lower-paid jobs by about the same number.
Voted for a law setting a six-month limit for deciding asylum appeals and hiring more officers to remove people whose claims fail.
Voted for a law lowering the residence needed for citizenship from eight years to six.
Voted against a law letting asylum seekers bring their families before a decision on their claims.
Voted for a law halting all asylum claims and refugee resettlement for four years and cutting work visas by half.
Voted for a law requiring detention of everyone who entered without permission until removal, with no time limit.
Voted for a law ending citizenship by birth for children of parents without legal status and removing permanent residence from anyone convicted of any offence.
Voted against a law allowing family reunification for recognized refugees.
Publicly urged fellow legislators to remove every resident without legal status within two years.
